assessment:
In this study, Song and colleagues investigate how the nematode C. elegans discriminates between familiar and novel bacterial food sources and how this recognition memory modulates feeding behavior. The authors demonstrate that worms increase their feeding rate on bacteria they have previously encountered compared to novel bacteria, and that this behavioral plasticity persists for at least 7-8 hours and requires a minimum of 9 hours of exposure to develop. This work addresses an important gap in understanding how familiarity discrimination—a form of recognition memory—regulates feeding across species, using C. elegans as a tractable model system.

The authors employ a multi-faceted experimental approach combining behavioral assays, genetic analysis, cell-specific rescue experiments, laser ablation, calcium imaging, and immunohistochemistry to dissect the neural circuit underlying this behavior. They identify a pathway in which recognition of familiar food activates ADF chemosensory neurons, which release serotonin that acts humorally to activate the SER-7 receptor in MC pharyngeal motor neurons, ultimately increasing feeding through enhanced cholinergic transmission to pharyngeal muscles. The conditioned media experiments provide mechanistic insight, suggesting that gustatory and/or olfactory cues from novel bacteria actively suppress this pathway. The work is technically sophisticated and employs appropriate controls for most experiments.

However, significant concerns raised during peer review temper confidence in some key conclusions. Reviewers note that day-to-day variability in baseline feeding rates (~100 pumps/min) is substantially larger than the familiarity effect itself (~20 pumps/min), raising questions about experimental design and whether all experiments and controls were conducted on the same day with identical reagents. The lack of complete pairwise bacterial comparisons (HB101 is always one member of each pair) limits assessment of generalizability. Additionally, several experiments showing no difference between conditions have 'control pumping rates on the very low side,' making it unclear whether further decreases could be detected, which affects interpretation of negative results from tph-1 and ser-7 mutants. The calcium imaging data, while supportive, lacks complete pairwise comparisons and detailed methodological information about baseline fluorescence ratios and photobleaching rates.

Despite these limitations, the study makes valuable contributions to understanding feeding regulation and familiarity discrimination in C. elegans. The identification of ADF as the critical serotonergic neuron (rather than NSM), the demonstration of humoral serotonin signaling, the localization of SER-7 action to MC neurons, and the discovery that novel food cues actively suppress the pathway all represent important advances. The work provides a foundation for future studies on the molecular mechanisms of familiarity discrimination and sensory integration, though some conclusions would benefit from additional validation with improved experimental controls for day-to-day variability.
